name: Very Light Brown
lede: Very Light Brown is a pale, dusty tan that our data files as a Japanese traditional color name, found in about one painting in eight in our archive.

sections.title: A steamed-chestnut tan
sections.body:
Our data traces this hue to the Japanese traditional color list as 蒸栗色 (Mushikuri-iro), literally "steamed chestnut color" [1]. The English label "Very Light Brown" comes from the xkcd 2010 crowd color survey, filed in our library at the same hex as the Japanese name [1][2]. No earlier dated listing survives in our sources, so 2010 is the first date we can give it [2].

Its nearest look-alikes are [[toupe]] (2.9 units, almost the same), [[sandstone]] (3.1, almost the same) and [[tan]] (3.2, slightly duller) [3]. [[maple]] and [[burlywood]] sit a touch further off, close enough to confuse at a glance [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this tan in 2,874 of 23,781 paintings, about 12.1 percent, as photographed; that puts it among the most common named colors we track, ahead of 95 percent of the rest [4]. It peaks in the 1400s, found in 8.9 percent of the 945 paintings we have from then (84 paintings), 1.1 times the expected rate for that century, and plays a light tone in 55 percent of the paintings that carry it [4]. John Singer Sargent uses it most, in 35 of his 287 works here [4]. It shows up most in Iranian paintings, at 4.1 times the baseline rate, and shares canvases more than chance with [[isabella-color]] and [[blanched-almond]] [4]. The earliest dated match is 799, a floor set by our archive's thin early centuries rather than a true first; that is 1,211 years before the English name's earliest record, so the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of any dye [4].
